e.etymology: A modern elaboration in the family of Aliana and Eliana, also read as Aly plus Anna. The spelling is especially popular in the Philippines.
From Arabic Tasnim, the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is promised to the righteous in the Quran (83:27).
An English surname from villages named Stratton, Old English straet, a paved Roman road, plus tun, settlement. It joined the run of surname names like Sutton and Paxton in the 2010s.

assoc.t: Stratton Oakmont, the firm in The Wolf of Wall Street

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayden, coined by American parents in the late 20th century from Jay and the -den ending of Braden and Hayden. It also overlaps with Jadon, a minor Old Testament name.
From Sanskrit ajaya, unconquered: a, not, plus jaya, victory. It is a common Hindu name across India; in the US it also appears as a spelled-out form of the initials A.J.
In Genesis Elam is a son of Shem and ancestor of the Elamites, whose ancient kingdom lay in what is now southwestern Iran. The meaning of the Hebrew name is uncertain.

assoc.t: Elam, ancient kingdom in what is now Iran

e.etymology: In Norway Aren is a variant of Arne, from Old Norse orn, eagle. In the US it is also an Armenian boys' name and a streamlined spelling of Aaron.
A short form of Beatrice and Beatrix, from Latin Viatrix, voyager, reshaped by beatus, blessed. Bea is now given as a full name as well.
namesakes: Bea Arthur (star of Maude and The Golden Girls)

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Ava, a medieval Germanic short name that is also treated as a form of Eve. Ava has been in the US top ten since 2005, which produced many alternate spellings.
A surname brought from the Netherlands and northern Germany, from a word for rich or powerful. As a first name it took off after Commander William Riker of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
namesakes: William Riker (first officer in Star Trek: The Next Generation)

assoc.t: Commander Riker of Star Trek: The Next Generation
Rikers Island, New York City's jail complex

e.note: Rikers Island is New York City's notorious jail, a strong association for many listeners.

e.etymology: A Spanish pet name, like Malena, formed from María Elena or from Magdalena. It is used on its own mainly in Mexican American families.
A compound of Ellie, a pet form of Eleanor, Ellen and Elizabeth, and Mae, a form of May or Mary. Written as one word it follows Southern double names like Ellamae and Annamae.

assoc.t: Elly May Clampett of The Beverly Hillbillies, by sound

e.etymology: From Latin Laurentius, a man from Laurentum, a town near Rome whose name may come from laurus, laurel. Saint Laurence was a 3rd-century Roman martyr. In French, Laurence is a women's name.
namesakes: Laurence Fishburne (actor, Morpheus in The Matrix)
Laurence Olivier (English stage and film actor)

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from a place in Lancashire, Old Norse ra, roe deer, plus skogr, wood. It was a popular American first name from the 1880s through the 1920s.
namesakes: Roscoe Arbuckle (silent film comedian known as Fatty Arbuckle)

assoc.t: roscoe, old gangster slang for a handgun

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 2000s combining the Ma- of Makayla and Mariah with Kiyah. It has no older source.
A recent American coinage that joins Brix, as in Brixton, to the -ley ending of Brinley and Paisley.

The French and German form of Teresa, a name first recorded in Spain and possibly from Greek therizein, to harvest, or the island of Thera. Saint Thérèse of Lisieux made this form popular with Catholics.
namesakes: Thérèse of Lisieux (French Carmelite saint known as the Little Flower)

e.etymology: From an English surname, a variant of Garrett, the medieval form of Gerard and Gerald, Germanic names built on ger, spear. It returned as a first name in the late 20th century.
A diminutive of Rosa, rose, with the Italian -ella ending; in America it was also heard as Rose plus Ella. It was most popular in the US around 1900.
A compound of Ella and Mae written as one word, a style common in the American South around 1900 and revived in the 2020s.
In Hebrew, Nava means beautiful or pleasant, a word used in the Song of Songs. A separate Persian Nava means melody or tune. Nava is also a Spanish surname from a word for a treeless plain.
A spelling of Elliott with a French-looking final e, used mostly for girls. Elliott is an English surname from a medieval pet form of Elias, the Greek form of Elijah, Hebrew for my God is Yahweh.
From Arabic din, religion or faith, the same word that ends names like Aladdin and Saladin. It sounds the same as the English name Dean.
The English word for a daydream, borrowed from French rêverie, from rêver, to dream. Its use as a name is very recent, helped by its nearness to Everly and Waverly.
A recent American coinage that blends Zaire, the former name of the Congo, with the A- opening of Azariah and Amari.
From Yiddish sheyne, beautiful, related to German schön, as in the phrase a shayne maydel, a lovely girl. In the US it also blended with Shana and Shanna from the 1970s on.
A transliteration of Yiddish sheyne, beautiful, a cousin of German schön. Shaina and Shayna are the same name; this spelling peaked in the US in 1987.
A spelling of Dakota, the name of the Dakota people of the northern plains, from their word dakhóta, ally or friend, and of two US states. It became a first name in the 1980s.

assoc.t: North Dakota and South Dakota, US states
the Dakota people, a Sioux nation

e.note: Dakota is the name of a living Native nation; some people consider its use as a baby name appropriative.

e.etymology: A Danish and Norwegian form of Ivar, from Old Norse Ívarr, usually explained as yew bow plus warrior. Scandinavian immigrants brought it to the Upper Midwest; Ivor is the British form.
A recent American blend of Nyla and the Hawaiian element lani, sky or heaven, in the style of Kailani and Leilani.
The French name Solène, long associated with Brittany and traced to Latin sollemnis, solemn or sacred, through Saint Solemnis, called Solenne in French, a bishop of Chartres around 500.
namesakes: Solène Marchand (Anne Hathaway's character in The Idea of You)

e.etymology: A 20th-century combination of Lee, from Old English leah, meadow, and Anne, from Hebrew Hannah, grace. It peaked in the US in 1969.
namesakes: Leanne Morgan (stand-up comedian and star of the Netflix sitcom Leanne)
